query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of boron into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy to promote in‐situ precipitation of high-entropy boride nanoprecipitates will enhance its mechanical integrity by impeding crack initiation and propagation, without degrading its intrinsic field-driven caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibiting a large caloric effect under applied-field and pressure-field operations but suffering from low fracture toughness and cracking.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition of boron (around 1–3 at%) during synthesis to induce in-situ formation of uniformly dispersed high-entropy boride nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Tested under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields as the original alloy, at temperatures and mechanical loading regimes comparable to prior epoxy and low-melting composite studies (e.g., compressive stresses up to ~200 MPa, and operating temperatures below the onset of phase instability).
generation.structural_mediator: High-entropy boride nanoprecipitates distributed along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The boride nanoprecipitates reinforce the microstructure by pinning dislocations and retarding crack propagation, thereby increasing compressive strength and toughness. Their presence is expected to be chemically and structurally compatible with the martensitic or magnetostructural transformations responsible for the caloric effect, so the field-induced caloric performance remains essentially unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in mechanical integrity is anticipated (e.g., a significant increase in compressive strength and crack resistance, potentially by at least 50% relative to the untreated alloy), while the magnitude of the applied-field or pressure-induced caloric response remains within 10% of that of the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that exhibits excellent caloric response but poor mechanical integrity and fracture resistance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under conditions where the operating fields (magnetic and pressure) and temperatures do not trigger additional phase instabilities; the boron content and processing parameters must be optimized such that the nanoprecipitate formation does not interfere with the mechanism of the caloric transformation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in strength and the degree to which the caloric response is maintained require empirical validation. There is also uncertainty regarding the optimal boron content and processing conditions to achieve a balanced microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with 1–3 at% boron addition to induce in-situ high-entropy boride precipitation, and a control set without boron. Process both sets under identical conditions. Subject the samples to identical applied magnetic and pressure fields and perform compressive loading tests alongside caloric effect measurements.
measurements: Compressive strength and fracture toughness (e.g., via standard compression tests up to ~200 MPa and crack propagation analysis)
Caloric response metrics such as isothermal entropy change
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to confirm the presence and dispersion of boride nanoprecipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant (e.g., >25%) improvement in mechanical robustness compared to the control, or if the caloric response is degraded by more than approximately 10%, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Rare-Earth-Zirconate Porous High-Entropy Ceramics with Unique Pore Structures for Thermal Insulating Applications

Abstract: Porous high-entropy ceramics are a new alternative material for thermal insulation. Their better stability and low thermal conductivity are due to lattice distortion and unique pore structures. In this work, rare-earth-zirconate ((La0.25Eu0.25Gd0.25Yb0.25)2(Zr0.75Ce0.25)2O7) porous high-entropy ceramics were fabricated by a tert-butyl alcohol (TBA)-based gel-casting method. The regulation of pore structures was realized through changing different initial solid loadings. The XRD, HRTEM, and SAED results showed that the porous high-entropy ceramics had a single fluorite phase without impurity phases, exhibiting high porosity (67.1–81.5%), relatively high compressive strength (1.02–6.45 MPa) and low thermal conductivity (0.0642–0.1213 W/(m·K)) at room temperature. Porous high-entropy ceramics with 81.5% porosity demonstrated excellent thermal properties, showing a thermal conductivity of 0.0642 W/(m·K) at room temperature and 0.1467 W/(m·K) at 1200 °C. High-Entropy Borides under Extreme Environment of Pressures and Temperatures

Abstract: AbstractThe high-entropy transition metal borides containing a random distribution of five or more constituent metallic elements offer novel opportunities in designing materials that show crystalline phase stability, high strength, and thermal oxidation resistance under extreme conditions. We present a comprehensive theoretical and experimental investigation of prototypical high-entropy boride (HEB) materials such as (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti)B2 and (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Zr)B2 under extreme environments of pressures and temperatures. The theoretical tools include modeling elastic properties by special quasi-random structures that predict a bulk modulus of 288 GPa and a shear modulus of 215 GPa at ambient conditions. HEB samples were synthesized under high pressures and high temperatures and studied to 9.5 GPa and 2273 K in a large-volume pressure cell. The thermal equation of state measurement yielded a bulk modulus of 276 GPa, in excellent agreement with theory.
